main.text: [III, 194] Chapter 11. [col. 408]
It is proved that the word קפוז kippoz, Es. XXXIV, 15, signifies neither the hedgehog, as the ancients thought, nor a kind of bird, as the moderns thought, but the serpent acontias, or iaculus.

In chapter 34 Isaiah threatens that Bozrah and Idumaea are to be laid waste by sword and fire, so that, all the inhabitants being either driven out or destroyed, it will thereafter be habitable only for wild and solitary animals. Among these is named קפוז kippoz, of which the divine Prophet speaks thus in verse 15: There shall kippoz nest, and shall be delivered, and shall break, and shall gather in its shadow. So the Hebrew runs word for word. But, taking the verbs תמלט, בקעה and דגרה from their general meaning to a special one, the more recent Hebrews rightly render this verse: There shall kippoz nest, and lay, and hatch, and brood in its shadow. For מלט malat in general is to deliver or to be delivered; here it is to bring forth, as in Es. LXVI, 7, המליטה זכר, where our version has, word for word, Elle a est è deliuree d' un masle, a phrase as much Hebrew as French. The Arabs also use the same verb ملط [malaṭa] malata of birth, but properly of one that is abortive and untimely. The Assyrian Venus, who, as Selden argues at length in his little book De Diis Syris, presided over childbirth and was the same as Lucina and Ilithyia, seems to have taken from this verb the name Μυλίττας [Mylittas], as it is in Herodotus, [col. 409] or Μυλήτας [Mylētas] and Μιλίτης [Militēs], as it is in Hesychius, rather than from the verb ילד, to beget, as Scaliger conjectures; for the meaning, like the sound of the word, agrees better. Lucina, after all, helps in childbirth, not in begetting. Likewise בקע in general is to split or to break; here it is to hatch the young by breaking the egg, as in Esa. LIX, 5: The eggs of the basilisk בקעו, they broke, that is, they hatched. So in Latin a chick is said to break out of the egg. Finally, דגר among the Chaldeans, from whom this verb was taken, is in general to gather; here it is to gather eggs or chicks under oneself, so that they may be kept warm by the mother's heat. It is taken no otherwise in Ier. XVII, 11, where the Prophet says קרא דגר ולא ילד, The partridge gathers (that is, broods) what it did not lay. Nor otherwise by the Chaldee translator, when he renders the Hebrew תחמם, she will warm, said of the ostrich's eggs, by תדגר, she will gather, that is, she will brood, Iob. XXXIX, 14 (var. 17). Moreover, on the words בקעה ודגרה, will hatch and brood, it should be noted that the conjunction and means the same as when or after, as if the Prophet had written, She will hatch the eggs after she has brooded them. So in Exod. XIV, 21: He made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided, that is, after the waters were divided. And in Esa. LXIV, 5: You were angry, and we sinned, that is, when we sinned, or because we sinned. So Kimchi. [III, 195] But these things are obvious to everyone; what קפוז kippoz is, is not, since no animal of this name occurs anywhere else, neither in Scripture, nor in the Talmud, nor in the books of the Syrians or Chaldeans. I shall, however, state what both the ancient and the more recent interpreters thought of this word. The Greeks, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Vulgate translator, Jerome, Pomarius and Schindler render it hedgehog, as if קפוז kippoz were the same as קפוד kippod a little before, in verse 11; persuaded, of course, by the closeness of sound and the easy interchange of the letters Z and D. Kimchi likewise, and Solomon, and Mordecai, and Aquinas, and nearly all the Hebrews there are, take kippod and kippoz for the same thing. But kippod, and therefore also kippoz, one explains as the tortoise, another as the little owl, another in general as a solitary bird. Aben Ezra alone, as far as I know, holds that kippod and kippoz are different birds, but of what kind he does not explain. And among those interpreters who in our own age have done useful work in producing new versions there is no small disagreement here. Santes explains it as hedgehog, Castalio as eagle-owl, Junius as blackbird, Diodati as il gufo, that is, scops owl; the English as the great Owe, that is, the great owl; the French, following Mercerus, as le martinet, that is, the swift; Arias inserts the Hebrew word itself into the Latin text, candidly confessing that he does not understand it.

Now, to state modestly but freely what I find lacking in each: first, I would have this held as certain, that קפוד kippod and קפוז kippoz, however similar in sound, are nevertheless names of different animals. 1. Because in the same sequence of the text they are presented by Isaiah as different. The pelican, he says, and the KIPPOD shall possess it. And, a few words later, There shall the KIPPOZ make its nest. This is an empty repetition if kippod and kippoz were the same ^{(1)}. 2. Above all this: whereas I have proved in its place ^{a)} that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog, that is, a viviparous quadruped, קפוז kippoz, on the contrary, is described as an oviparous animal ^{(2)}: There shall the kippoz make its nest, and lay, and hatch (the eggs, that is), after it has (them) warmed in its shadow. What could be more explicit? Thus Santes and Schindlerus in their Lexicons, under the word בקע, seem plainly not to have known what kind of animal the hedgehog is; otherwise they would never have said, as they do in expounding this passage, that the hedgehog builds a nest, and breaks its eggs, and, when they are broken, hatches its young. [III, 196] Secondly, whatever קפוז kippoz may be, since it takes its name from leaping, it is neither the tortoise nor the bird cypselus. For leaping suits neither. Not the tortoise, which does not even walk except by crawling. Nor the bird cypselus, which others call apus, because it lacks the use of its feet and is almost incapable of walking. Pliny [col. 410] book 10, ch. 39: Those called apodes fly most of all, because they lack the use of their feet; by others they are called cypseli, of the swallow kind. Also: They have no rest except in the nest. They either hang or lie. Others too write the same. Moreover, since the cypselus is a sea bird, or a bird of the riverbanks, why should it be said to nest in the dry places of Idumaea? Mercerus urges in vain that the word cypselus is not far from the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. For that counts for little when the other marks are lacking. Not to mention that a word plainly of Greek origin is wrongly derived from the Hebrew language. For cypseli are so called ἀπὸ τῶν κυψελίδων [apo tōn kypselidōn], from the little cells which they build for themselves out of mud. The Philosopher, History, book 9, ch. 30: Οἱ δὲ ἄποδες, οὓς καλοῦσί τινες κυψέλους, νεοττεύουσιν ἐν κυψελίσιν ἐν πυλοῦ πεπλασμένας μακραῖς [Hoi de apodes, hous kalousi tines kypselous, neotteuousin en kypselisin en pylou peplasmenas makrais]. So in Herodotus, in Terpsichore, the son of Eëtion is given the name Cypselus, ἀπὸ τῆς κυψέλης [apo tēs kypselēs], in which he had lain hidden and escaped the danger of death.

The third interpretation, which explains קפוז kippoz as the blackbird, has more probability. 1. For blackbird in Greek is κόσσυφος [kossyphos], which could seem to have been formed from the Hebrew kipphoz, as the ancients pronounced it, by a metathesis of letters. 2. And it seems it can be reckoned among the solitary animals, since Varro ^{b)}, Festus ^{c)} and Isidore ^{d)} would have merula [blackbird] so called because it flies mera (that is, alone). 3. The same bird could rightly be called קפוז kippoz from leaping, since it hops rather than walks. Pliny book 10, ch. 38: Some birds walk, like crows; some hop, like sparrows and blackbirds. These were Junius's reasons for rendering kippoz as blackbird. But that most learned man did not consider that the Prophet is there dealing with φιλερήμοις [philerēmois] animals, desert-loving ones, by whose habitation a place formerly cultivated becomes waste and dreadful. No one would say the blackbird is of that number: it is a harmless bird, comely in form, sweet of voice, pleasant in taste, its dung most useful for enriching fields, so much so that Varro book 3, On Agriculture, ch. 5, wants it kept in aviaries together with nightingales. They do indeed say it is called merula because it usually wanders alone and does not usually associate with birds of its own kind except for the sake of its brood. But this derivation, along with others of Varro's, is ridiculed by Quintilian book 1, ch. 5: Who, he says, would not be pardoned after Varro? who wanted to persuade Cicero (for he writes to him) that ager [field] was so called because something agitur [is done] in it, and graculi [jackdaws] because they fly gregatim [in flocks]; although it is manifest that the one comes from the Greek, the other from the cries of the birds. But it was worth so much to him to make the turn, that merula, because it flies alone, was named as if mera volans [flying alone] [III, 197]. And indeed that merula is said as if merivola is pure invention; yet merula could have been said for mera, that is, alone, as a diminutive. But wherever it got its name, there is no one who does not know that it lives in inhabited places, and that one species of blackbird mostly frequents ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων [epi tōn keramōn], upon the tiles of roofs, as the Philosopher observes in History, book 9, chapter 19. Hence some refer here that saying of the Psalmist: I was like a solitary sparrow upon the roof.

This difficulty was avoided by the late Diodati (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), who renders קפוז kippoz in Italian as gufo, that is, scops [scops-owl]: a bird not only solitary and φιλέρημον [philerēmon], but also nocturnal, ugly and ill-omened, with a harsh and discordant voice ^{(3)}. The old Scholiast of Homer: Σκῶπες· ὄρνεα νυκτίνομα, κακόνομα, κακόφωνα, οἱονεὶ σκαιόπές τινες [Skōpes· ornea nyktinoma, kakonoma, kakophōna, hoionei skaiopes tines]. 2. Add that the name קפוז kippoz, that is, little leaper, seems fitly applicable to a bird that so delights in dancing that, when the fowler dances, it is reported to be caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē], that is, dancing in return opposite him. Accordingly Athenaeus ^{e)} counts the scops among the animals which, watching a dancer, νευροσπαστεῖται [neurospasteitai], that is, are moved like puppets νευροσπαστῶν [neurospastōn] (in French des marionettes), and like — a piece of wood moved by another's strings. Hence σκὼψ [skōps] ^{f)} is the name of a kind of dance, notable for its variety of movements and gestures. And σκώπτειν [skōptein] properly means to mimic something with ridiculous imitation, like the scops-owls. 3. Moreover, [col. 411] for scops the ancients mostly wrote cops ^{g)}, without the prefixed Sigma. Among them are Epicharmus, Speusippus, Metrodorus and Alexander of Myndus, who asserts that Homer and Aristotle too wrote κῶπες [kōpes], not σκῶπες [skōpes]. We note this because κῶψ [kōps] comes closer to the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. And the Italian word gufo seems derivable from either, since gli cufi, or gufi, are the copes or scopes of the ancients. Phavorinus: καὶ δοκοῦσι σκῶπες εἶναι, οὓς κούφους ἢ γούφους οἱ Ῥωμαῖοί φασι [kai dokousi skōpes einai, hous kouphous ē gouphous hoi Rhōmaioi phasi]. The same is in Eustathius, except that, instead of κούφους ἢ γούφους [kouphous ē gouphous], our copies wrongly read κουκούβας [koukoubas]. The judicious reader sees that this last interpretation is by far the most probable. Nor, I think, did those mean anything else who rendered the same word eagle-owl, or great owl. Yet this is certain: the scops [III, 198] could not have been called קפוז kippoz because it is ὀρχηστικὴ [orchēstikē] and is caught ἀντορχουμένη [antorchoumenē] by a dancing fowler. For the Hebrew קפז is not ὀρχεῖσθαι [orcheisthai], but ἅλλεσθαι [hallesthai]. We have learned the proper use of the word from the Arabs, who use three nearly synonymous verbs, زج [zj] zaggia, طفر [ṭafara] taphara (in Chaldee טפז tephaz) and قفز [qafaza] kaphaza (in Chaldee קפז kephaz), so interchangeably that زج [zj] zaggia mostly means to leap forward on level ground, طفر [ṭafara] taphara to leap down from a high place to a lower one, قفز [qafaza] kaphaza to leap upward from a lower place. Hence in Avicenna's chapter ^{h)} On the kinds of exercise, القفز [al-qafz] Alcaphzo is done الي شي ليتعلق به [ilā shayʾ li-yataʿallaqa bihi] toward some object, so that one may hang from it. And in the sacred paraphrases قفز [qafaza] kaphaza occurs everywhere for the Hebrew verbs דלג, זנק and נתר, which are known to signify ἅλμα [halma] and πήδημα [pēdēma], not ὄρχησιν [orchēsin]. Therefore קפוז kippoz, if the thing is to answer to the name, must be an animal ἁλτικὸν [haltikon], not ὀρχηστικὸν [orchēstikon] (in French propre a sauter, non a dancer). How much these two differ, everyone sees. Nor was this overlooked by Scaliger, who, explaining the passage of Aristotle where the otus is said to be ἀντορχούμενος [antorchoumenos], History book 8, ch. 12, says: Ἀντορχούμενος [Antorchoumenos], gesticulating in return. Ὄρχησις [Orchēsis] is something other than ἅλμα [halma].

Therefore, since קפוז kippoz has hitherto been sought in vain both among the birds and among the quadrupeds, let the learned judge whether it does not rather belong to the serpents, among which is the acontias or iaculus, so called διὰ τὸ ὁρμᾶν ὥσπερ τὰ ἀκόντια [dia to horman hōsper ta akontia], because it rushes forward like javelins. So the Scholiast on Nicander. Not very differently Aelian, book 6, ch. 18: Ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἀκοντίων δίκην ἑαυτόν τις μεθίησι, καὶ ἐπιφέρεται. καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἐξ οὗ δρᾷ ἔχει· κέκληται γὰρ Ἀκοντίας [Ēdē de kai akontiōn dikēn heauton tis methiēsi, kai epipheretai. kai to onoma ex hou dra echei; keklētai gar Akontias]. There is also a certain serpent which launches itself like a javelin (Apostolius ^{i)} reads μεθίστησι [methistēsi], transfers) and rushes upon its prey; and it has its name from what it does, for it is called Iaculus. Accordingly almost all ascribe to it ἅλμα [halma] and προσπήδησιν [prospēdēsin]. Agatharchides, ch. 50, on this kind of serpent: Τὴν πληγὴν δὲ δίδωσι παλλόμενον εἰς ὕψος [Tēn plēgēn de didōsi pallomenon eis hypsos]; It strikes its blow when hurled aloft. This can be accepted. Yet later writers consistently write ἁλλόμενον [hallomenon]. Artemidorus in Strabo, book 16: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι [Opheis de spithamiaioi, phoinikoi tēn chroan, prosallomenoi], etc. There are serpents three palms long, of a scarlet colour, leaping at one, etc. Diodorus, book 3, p. 126: Δάκνουσι δὲ προσπηδῶντες, καὶ ἁλλόμενοι πρὸς ὕψος [Daknousi de prospēdōntes, kai hallomenoi pros hypsos]; They bite, springing forward and leaping aloft. Aelian, History, book 8, ch. 13: Ἔστι ἁλτικὸν θηρίον, καὶ διαπηδῆσαι καὶ εἴκοσιν εἰ δέοι, πήχεις οἷόν τε [Esti haltikon thērion, kai diapēdēsai kai eikosin ei deoi, pēcheis hoion te]; It is a serpent strong at leaping, and able, if need be, to leap across a distance of twenty cubits. Galen, ch. 8 of To Piso: Ὁ [III, 199] δὲ ἀκοντίας, ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν πάνυ, καὶ ὥς πέρ τι ἀκόντιον ἐφαλλόμενος τοῖς [col. 412] σώμασιν [Ho de akontias, ekteinas heauton pany, kai hōs per ti akontion ephallomenos tois sōmasin]; The iaculus, stretching itself out greatly and leaping upon bodies like a javelin. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, ch. 4: They leap up into trees, and when some animal comes their way, they throw themselves upon it. And Avicenna ^{k)}, vol. 2, p. 139: ربما كمنت علي الاشجار راصدة وترمي بانفسها علي من يمر بها وتثب منزجة اليه [rubbamā kamanat ʿalī al-ashjār rāṣidatan wa-tarmī bi-anfusihā ʿalī man yamurru bihā wa-tathibu manzajatan ilayhi] Sometimes it lies in ambush up in trees; and if anyone passes near them, it hurls itself and, leaping down, rushes upon him. Hence it is that the acontias is called in Arabic by Avicenna قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara, as if you were to say the one that leaps at and the one that leaps down. For قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza is properly said when it strives upward, say from the ground into trees; and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara when it leaps down from on high, say from the trees onto travellers. The former name is formed entirely after the pattern of the Hebrew קפוז kippoz, or kipphoz, as it is certain the ancients read and pronounced it. The radical letters are the same in both, and the form of the noun nearly the same, so far as the difference of the languages allowed. Only in the Arabic قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza a feminine ending has been added, which is lacking in the noun קפוז kippoz, as the four feminine verbs joined to it show. The ending differs, however, because the Hebrew word for serpent, נחש, is masculine, and the Arabic حية [ḥayya] feminine ^{(4)}.

So much for the word. As for the thing: among the plagues of Africa none is worse than this serpent. Aëtius, in the place cited above, ch. 27: From its bite follow all the things said of the viper, and even worse ones. Avicenna: From its bite there arise violent pain and a hot ulcer over the whole body, and from it death. And Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo write that its bite is ἀνίατον [aniaton] or ἀνήκεστον [anēkeston], that is, incurable. Accordingly in Agatharchides this kind of serpent is said to be ἰωδέστατον πάντων [iōdestaton pantōn], the most poisonous of all. For he seems to have written thus, not ἰδιώτατον [idiōtaton], as our editions have it. Nor can this missile be avoided, since it bursts from ambush with such force that it outstrips all flight. It flies as if from a missile-engine, [III, 200] says Pliny; and Solinus says that, whirled from the trees with the greatest force, it pierces whatever animal fortune has put in its way. And Aelian: Ἁλλόμενον δὲ παραχρῆμα ἐνέφυ [Hallomenon de parachrēma enephy], Leaping, it clings at once, namely to whatever it attacks with its leap. Such headlong speed is described thus by Lucan, book 9, line 822.

Behold! far off, from the wood of a barren trunk, a savage serpent (Africa calls it the iaculus) twisted and hurled itself, and passed through the head and pierced temples of Paulus. No poison does its work there; death seized him with the wound. Then it was found how slowly the stones that the sling whirls fly, how sluggishly the air hisses with the Scythian arrow.

There are some who infer that this serpent manages only a slight leap and does not rise above a man's flanks, from these words of Strabo in the Latin version: "Serpents also, a span long, of a purple colour, leaping up as far as the flanks, whose bite is incurable". But they are misled by a faulty version, and this arose from a faulty punctuation of the Greek text, which reads thus: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι καὶ μέχρι λαγόνος, τὸ δῆγμα ἔχοντες ἀνήκεστον· [Opheis de spithamiaioi, phoinikoi tēn chroan, prosallomenoi kai mechri lagonos, to dēgma echontes anēkeston]. It should be read προβαλλόμενοι, καὶ μέχρι λαγόνος τὸ δῆγμα [proballomenoi, kai mechri lagonos to dēgma], etc. For the sense is not that they leap as far as the flanks, but that the wounds they inflict by their spring are incurable over the whole body as far as the flanks, whereas otherwise they can be healed, namely if they are below the flanks, say on the shins or thighs. For Strabo took this from Artemidorus, and Artemidorus from Agatharchides, whose words are: Δῆγμα δὲ ἀνίατον, ἂν τὸν λαγόνος ἀνώτερον αἱμάξῃ· [Dēgma de aniaton, an ton lagonos anōteron haimaxē]; "The bite is incurable when it wounds above the flanks." Thus the iaculus of which Lucan speaks not only raised itself by its leap to the flanks, but [col. 413]
"Through the head of Paulus, and through the pierced temples, it flew."

And in Isidore the iaculi "leap up into trees"; and in Aelian they leap across καὶ εἴκοσιν, εἰ δέοι, πήχεις [kai eikosin, ei deoi, pēcheis], "even twenty cubits, if need be"; and for such a length of leap the height must be proportionately equal. From this the reader understands that the places which abound in such a pest must be utterly vast and desolate. And this is what Isaiah means when he writes that the acontias will not only lodge in Idumaea, but will also give birth there and hatch the eggs on which it has brooded. If anyone denies that this kind of Libyan serpent was known to the Jews or the Idumaeans, let him hear these words of Marcellinus in book 22: "Egypt also nourishes innumerable serpents, raging beyond all destruction: basilisks, and amphisbaenas, and scytalae, and acontiae." Others assign them to Arabia. Lucan, book 6, line 677:
"Not the winged serpent of the Arabs": — —
that is, the iaculus. For the same poet says in book 9, line 720:
[III, 201] "And the natrix, violator of water, and the winged iaculi."
To say nothing of Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo, who describe them among the Sabaeans, to whom the Jews had begun to sail already from the age of Solomon.

But to make the matter clearer, it is worth weighing Isaiah's words one by one. There], he says, that is, in Idumaea, a part of Arabia adjoining Egypt, in which Ammianus describes acontias serpents. The kippoz shall nest], that is, the iaculus or acontias, called from its leap קפוז kippoz in Hebrew, as in Arabic قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza. I admit that to nest is most properly said of birds, as a very learned man once objected to me; but nest is also applied καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs] to other animals. 1. To man, for instance, as in Eccles. XXXVI, 28. Τίς γὰρ πιστεύσει, etc. ἀνθρώπῳ μὴ ἔχοντι νοσσιὰν, καὶ καταλύοντι οὗ ἐὰν ὀψίσῃ· [Tis gar pisteusei, etc. anthrōpō mē echonti nossian, kai katalyonti hou ean opsisē]; "Who will trust a man who has no nest, and lodges wherever evening overtakes him?" Hence Iob. XXIX, 18. "I shall die in my nest." Num. XXIV, 21. of the Kenite: "You have set your nest in the rock." Ierem. XLIX, 16. and Abd. 11. of the Idumaean: "Though you should set your nest as high as the eagle." Hab. II, 9. "Woe to him who gapes after evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high!" 2. To the lion, in the Greek version of Nahum II, 12. Ἔπλησε θήρας νοσσιὰν αὐτοῦ [Eplēse thēras nossian autou], "He filled his nest with prey." Hebr. חריו, "his holes." Alcamus: العرزال عريسة الاسد وما يجمعه في ماوا هلاشباله مما يمهده كالعش [al-ʿirzāl ʿarīsat al-asad wa-mā yajmaʿuhu fī māwā hlʾshbālh mimmā yumahhiduhu ka-l-ʿushsh] Alirzal, "the lion's den, and what he gathers in his lair for his cubs, to spread beneath them as a nest." 3. To the pig. Columella, book 8, ch. 9: "In its own sty each litter waits for its mother" (nidus), that is, the piglets lying in the pen as in a nest. 4. To the porcupine. Callimachus, in the Hymn to Artemis:
Καὶ κοίτην ἐλάφοιο, καὶ ὕστρικος ἔνθα καλιαὶ, [Kai koitēn elaphoio, kai hystrikos entha kaliai,]

"And the lair of the stag, and where the nests of the porcupine are." 5. To the hedgehog. Esa. XIII, 22. Καὶ νοσσοποιήσουσιν ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις αὐτῶν· [Kai nossopoiēsousin echinoi en tois oikois autōn]; "And hedgehogs shall make nests in their houses." Isaac [Tzetzes] on Lycophron, line 1093: "The hedgehog, since it knows in advance which winds are going to blow," ἀποφράττει τὸ πρὸς τὸν μέλλοντα πνεῖν μέρος τῆς καλιᾶς αὐτοῦ, ὑπανοίγει δὲ τὸ ἕτερον [apophrattei to pros ton mellonta pnein meros tēs kalias autou, hypanoigei de to heteron], "blocks the part of its nest facing the wind that is about to blow, and opens the other." 6. To the fish phycis, of which Pliny, book 9, ch. 26: "It alone among fishes makes a nest of seaweed, and gives birth in the nest." And Ovid in the Halieutica:
"And imitating beneath the waves the sweet nests of birds."

7. To the crocodile. Solinus: By natural providence it marks out a place for its nest. 8. To worms. Thus Pliny, book 11, ch. 28, says that little worms nest in dung. 9. To the gnat, the fly, the bee, the wasp and the hornet. Lucian in the Praise of the Fly: Νεοττίαν δὲ, ἢ καλιὰν, [col. 414] [III, 202] οὐκ ἐνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο [Neottian de, ē kalian, ouk eni topō katestēsato]; But it has not set up its nest, or little nest, in a single place. And in the Icaromenippus: Ἅπαντα διαγινώσκεις τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς· τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, τὰ θηρία, μικροῦ δεῖν, τὰς τῶν ἐμπίδων νεοττίας [Hapanta diaginōskeis ta epi gēs; tous anthrōpous, ta thēria, mikrou dein, tas tōn empidōn neottias]; You discern all things that are on earth: men, beasts and, I might almost say, the nests of gnats. Josephus on Samson, Antiquities, book 5, ch. 10: Ἐπιτυγχάνει σμήνει μελισσῶν, ἐν τῷ στήθει τοῦ λέοντος ἐκείνου νενοσσευκότων [Epitynchanei smēnei melissōn, en tō stēthei tou leontos ekeinou nenosseukotōn]; He came upon a swarm of bees which had nested in the breast of that lion. The Chaldee paraphrase of Iudic. XIV, 8: והא קנא דדבריתא בפגרא דאריא, And behold, a nest of bees in the carcass of the lion! And the Arabic: واذا في صدر الاسد نحل قد عششت هناك وقد سال العسل من عش النحل [wa-idhā fī ṣadr al-asad naḥl qad ʿashshashat hunāka wa-qad sāla al-ʿasal min ʿushsh al-naḥl] And behold, in the breast of the lion bees which had nested there, and honey was flowing from the bees' nest. So too 1 Sam. XIV, 26. The honey was flowing down من عش النحل [min ʿushsh al-naḥl] from the bees' nest. And the Chaldee again in the following verse: He stretched out the end of the staff that he had in his hand and dipped it בקינא דדובשא, in the nest of honey. Virgil, Georgics book 4, on bees:
They cherish their offspring and their nests. — —

Pliny, book 11, ch. 21: Wasps make their nests of mud up on high, and their wax in them; hornets in caves and underground. And again: The wasps that are called ichneumons kill one kind of spider, called the phalangium, and carry it into their nests. Likewise, on hornets: In spring they make nests, generally with four doors, in which the workers are bred. When these have been reared, they then build other, larger nests, in which they bring forth the future mothers. And ch. 22, on silkworms: They form nests of mud in the shape of salt, fixed to a stone, of such hardness that they can hardly be pierced with spear-points. Epiphanius, Heresy 44, on the kind of wasp they call ζώπυρον [zōpyron]: Ἐπὰν δέ τις διερχόμενος τὸν αὐτοῦ φωλεὸν, ἢ καλιὰν, καθέλοι [Epan de tis dierchomenos ton autou phōleon, ē kalian, katheloi]; If a traveller destroys its lair and nest. The ζώπυρον [zōpyron] is in Chaldee זיבורא zibbora, and the Arabs' زنبور [zunbūr] zanbur, of which Damir says: يتخذ عشه تحت الارض [yattakhidhu ʿushshahu taḥta al-arḍ] It takes its nest for itself under the earth. 10. To ants. Thus in the Talmudic tractate Nedarim you read קיני דשומשמני, nests of ants. And in Horus, book 2, ch. 60: Τιθεμένων (νυκτερίδος) τῶν πτερῶν εἰς τὴν νεοσσίαν τῶν μυρμήκων, οὐ προσέρχεται αὐτῶν τις [Tithemenōn (nykteridos) tōn pterōn eis tēn neossian tōn myrmēkōn, ou proserchetai autōn tis]; When a bat's wings are placed at the nests of ants, not one of them comes out. And Apuleius, book 8: In whose very rotten trunk the nests of the ants dwelling there were swarming (var. bubbling). 11. To mice and other small animals. Minucius Felix: Mice, etc., unless you drive them away, nest in the very mouth of your god. And Arnobius, book 6: Do you not see that under the bases (var. hollows) of these images geckos, shrews, mice and light-shunning cockroaches make their nests [III, 203] and dwell? 12. To locusts. Hence, when David complains that he has been shaken off like a locust, Psalm. CIX, 23, Kimchi and Aben Ezra observe that it refers to a locust שאין לו קן, which has no nest. And Damir, after saying that the locust, when about to bring forth, beats the hardest rocks with its tail until they open in a crack, and lays its eggs in that crack, adds: فيكون له كالافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا [fa-yakūnu lahu ka-l-ufḥūṣ wa-yakūnu ḥāḍinan lahā wa-murabbiyan] And (this crack) serves them as a nest, in which they cherish and rear their young. 13. Finally, it is certain that nests are not seldom attributed to serpents. Cic., On Divination, book 2: That there was a snake in the cradle is not so wonderful, especially in Solonium (which is a plain in the territory of Lanuvium), where snakes are wont to nest by the hearth. Some wrongly read nundinari [to hold market]. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 16: Ὅταν ἐπὶ [col. 415] τὴν πηγὴν τὸ ὕδωρ πιεῖν ἔλθῃ ὁ ὄφις, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [Hotan epi tēn pēgēn to hydōr piein elthē ho ophis, ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai]; When the serpent comes to the spring to drink, it does not carry its poison with it, but, having left it in its nest, approaches thus pure. In its nest, that is, ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ [en tō phōleō], in its lair, as the same author has it in the Heresy of the Ophites, ch. 8. R. Selomo, explaining what the hole of the asp is in Esa. XI, 8, says that it is a hole in the earth שהנחש מקנן בתוכו, in the midst of which the serpent nests. And the Arabic translator in the same place has for hole of the asp عش الافاعي [ʿushsh al-afāʿī], the nest of vipers.

Now what follows in Isaiah, There shall the acontias nest, and lay, and hatch out the eggs, which it has kept warm in its shadow, are the very words which the naturalists use on this subject. The Philosopher, on serpents, History book 5, at the end: Ὠοτοκοῦσιν ἔξω· ὅταν δὲ τέκῃ, εἰς τὴν γὴν ἐπωάζει. ἐκλέπεται δὲ καὶ ταῦτα τῷ ὑστέρῳ ἔτει [Ōotokousin exō; hotan de tekē, eis tēn gēn epōazei. eklepetai de kai tauta tō hysterō etei]. They lay their eggs outside; when they have laid them, they keep them warm in the ground. And these are hatched in the following year. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 62: Serpents lay eggs, etc. And they incubate them woven together in the ground, and hatch the young in the following year. And Celsus, book 5, ch. 27: They (serpents) are most deadly when they are incubating. Therefore in Isaiah מלט is ὠοτοκεῖν [ōotokein], to lay eggs; דגר is ἐπωάζειν [epōazein], to keep warm, to incubate; בקע is ἐκλέπειν [eklepein], to hatch out. And Isaiah himself elsewhere expresses with the same verb the hatching of the eggs of the basilisk, as we noted above ^{l)}.

Also the verb דגר, properly to gather together, or to keep warm eggs gathered and joined together, although it is applied to birds, nevertheless fits a serpent best of all, whose eggs are not only collected together but also cling to one another by a mutual bond, like a necklace. [III, 204] Aristotle, in the place cited above: Τὰ δ' ὠὰ ἀλλήλοις συνεχῆ ἐστιν, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν γυναικῶν ὑποδερίδες [Ta d' ōa allēlois synechē estin, hōsper hai tōn gynaikōn hypoderides]; The eggs are joined to one another like women's necklaces, that is, like the pearls in necklaces. Damir too, after describing the eggs of the serpent as long, of a dusky, green, black, white or variegated colour, marked with certain spots, shining (though the cause of such great variety is not sufficiently apparent), and after treating also of the fluid hidden inside, says: وهو في جوفها منضد طولا علي خط واحد [wa-huwa fī jawfihā munaḍḍad ṭūlan ʿalī khaṭṭ wāḥid] Through the belly they are joined lengthwise along a single line. And Scaliger: We have seen these eggs glued to one another, in the manner of the little beads with which women count their prayers. There are some who think that this is called in Hebrew שלל של ביצים, but properly שלל של ביצים is the clustering of the eggs in the hen's belly, when they are approaching maturity. Just as the smaller eggs, first clustered together from the seed, are called אשכול של ביצים, a cluster of eggs. See the Talmudists in the tractate Betsa, fol. 7a.

Nor should it be passed over that the Prophet says the acontias keeps its eggs warm בצלה, in its shadow, whereas he would rather have said under its wings, or under its feathers, or under the shadow of its wings, if the subject were a bird. Perhaps also by these very words the divine seer hints that this kind of serpent is especially solicitous for its eggs. At least the amphisbaena, which Avicenna suspects is a species of iaculus, is described in Albertus as a serpent that is watchful, and very solicitous for its eggs when it incubates them ^{(5)}.

notes.text: This argument is little weakened by the variant reading, since six codices cited by Kennicott have קפוד for קפוז. For the matter itself shows that it is a slip of the pen which, committed by one scribe, soon passed into several codices as well.

Because he did not weigh this very point, JO. ERN. FABER, in his dissertation On the animals mentioned in Zephan. II, 12., wrongly interprets קפוז as hystrix [porcupine], calling the Ethiopic קנפוז to his aid.
Athen. book 9, ch. 10. Aelian, Histor. book 15, ch. 28. Eustath. on Odyss. ι.
Athen. book 14. Pollux book 4, ch. 14. Aelian and Eustath., as above.
See Athen. book 9. Homer, Odyss. ε. Arist. Hist. book 9, ch. 28.

That the σκῶπα [skōpa] of the ancients is to be referred to the strix [owl] called scops by Linnaeus (Syst. vol. 1, p. 290, 13th ed.) is shown by BUFFON in the Hist. Avium, vol. 3, p. 51 of the Berlin translation. In Theocritus, Id. 1, v. 136, SCHREBER too, a most eminent man, interprets σκωπας [skōpas] in the Harles edition as the striges scopes of Linnaeus. Cf. also Aldrovandi, Ornithol. book 8, ch. 4, and SCHNEIDER on Aelian, Hist. Animal. book 15, ch. 28.

BELLONIUS, in his Singularia, book 2, ch. 14 (where he also gives a picture of this serpent), writes that he saw an iaculus on Rhodes, marked with tiny spots, no larger than a lentil, black and round, each surrounded like an eye by a white ring, such as appear on the small torpedo-fish. It is, he says, three palms long, no thicker than the little finger; its colour is ash-grey, approaching the colour of milk, and under the belly it is entirely white; it has scales along the back and plates along the belly, arranged as in the rest of the serpent kind. The neck is blackish above, marked with two white lines which begin at the head and run along the whole back right to the tail.

To TYCHSEN, on the Physiolog. Syr. Chapter 23, §. 2, p. 126, קפוז seems to be the strix aluco or strix ulula, led by no other argument than that this bird utters a call, Kewits, similar to the name Kippots. How much strength there is in this argument, everyone will understand for himself.
